speedInfo: The mission compresses one Titan day, about 16 Earth days, into {minutes} minutes. Driving is compressed too: rovers in this game drive {compression} times faster than the real speeds their parts are modeled on.

On Apollo 15 in 1971, the crew reported that about 6 to 7 km/h was the most comfortable driving speed for the Lunar Roving Vehicle. Its top speed was of the order of 9 to 13 km/h, depending on slope, roughness, and soil.

Robotic rovers drive far slower. NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars have a top speed of about 4 cm/s (0.15 km/h) on flat ground. Dragonfly, the real Titan mission, will fly instead of driving.

landing.heading: Landing: Shangri-La dunes
landing.briefing: The lander has touched down on a firm interdune corridor in the Shangri-La dune field on Titan, Saturn's largest moon. The rover is deploying.

ticket.briefing: REL secures a spot for the rover on the next launch to Titan. The lander will set it down on a firm interdune corridor in the Shangri-La dunes.

story.site: The program's last rover goes to the Shangri-La dunes on Titan, Saturn's largest moon. The dune sand is thought to be organic material, and nobody has sampled it yet. Nearby Selk crater may once have held liquid water mixed with organic material, and NASA's Dragonfly mission is headed for this region.
sources: Lorenz et al. (2021), Selection and characteristics of the Dragonfly landing site near Selk crater, Titan, Planet. Sci. J. 2:24, doi:10.3847/PSJ/abd08f

design.title: Mission 3: Titan
body: The campaign ends on Titan, Saturn's largest moon, in the Shangri-La dune field. The balance carried over from Mars is {balance}.
Parts and launch ticket tiers are the same as on the Moon in this version: {tiers}.

This is the last mission, and its goal is to survive: the rover must still be running at the end of the {minutes} minutes. A sleeping rover counts as running. The balance does not decide it. If the rover is lost, Titan can be tried again from the start of the Titan round, or the campaign can end there.

design.title: No useful sunlight
body: Titan's thick orange haze lets very little sunlight reach the ground. Solar panels give almost no power there, so in this version the rover runs on its battery alone.
The battery is the energy budget for the whole mission. Driving, staying awake and the lights all draw on it, and nothing refills it. The specification sheet shows the range on one battery.
Every rover still needs a part in the power slot. At Titan the cheaper panel does as well as the mast: both earn almost nothing.

design.title: Always cold
body: Titan is about −179 °C, day and night, everywhere on the map. The cold never lets up: when the cold meter is full, the rover freezes.

Awake, the rover's own electronics and a heater keep it warm, and the cold meter stays low. Asleep, only the heater fights the cold, so the rover cools. Rain cools every rover faster. Without a heater, the rover freezes before the mission ends.
Lights let the rover drive through the long night, at a high battery cost. Without lights it can only wait or sleep until dawn.

drive.title: One Titan day
body: W A S D or arrow keys to drive. Space to brake. P to power down or power up.

The mission lasts {minutes} minutes and covers one Titan day, about 16 Earth days. It starts in the morning: about {dayLeftMinutes} minutes of daylight, then a {nightMinutes}-minute night, then dawn for the last {dawnMinutes} minutes. There is no clock: the Sun is a faint disc behind the haze.
Dark dune sand is soft, and the wheels can dig in. The bright interdune corridors are firm.

drive.title: Energy and the long night
body: The energy bar is the battery, and the panel adds almost nothing. When it reaches zero, the mission ends.

At sunset, choose. Lights on: the rover keeps driving, at a high battery cost. Sleep: power down with P; the battery drains slowly and the rover wakes by itself at dawn. A rover without lights cannot drive at night.
Asleep at night, time passes {nightClockRate} times faster, so the long night goes by quickly.

drive.title: Sleep saves energy, but the rover cools
body: The cold never lets up. Awake, the electronics and the heater keep the rover warm, and driving adds a little more heat. Asleep, in the rain, or without a heater, the rover cools and the cold meter climbs.
Watch the cold meter while the rover sleeps. Power up with P to warm it again, at an energy cost.
Hard impacts and ground steeper than {maxSlope}° damage the rover, as on the Moon.

drive.title: Methane rainstorm
body: One methane rainstorm crosses the site during the mission. The lander's weather station forecasts it about {rainWarningSeconds} s ahead, and it lasts about {rainSeconds} s.
In the rain, visibility closes in, photographs do not count, and the cold rises faster. Park on known ground, or keep to a route the rover has already driven.

drive.title: Instruments and map

instrument.camera: Camera: {key} (or its button) takes a photograph. The Dune sea photograph counts from a dune crest viewpoint, looking out over the dune field.
instrument.drill: Drill: stop the rover, then press {key} (or its button) to drill a sample. Samples count at up to three sites, each at least {sampleSpacing} m from the lander and from each other. A first sample in the Selk ejecta field is a record.

body: Each instrument in the payload bay has a number key, 1 to {bayMax} in bay order, and a button beside the meters.
The engineering notebook records what the mission teaches about the rover. Open it with N or the Notebook button; the mission pauses while it is open, and Escape closes it.

The map starts zoomed in on the lander and widens as the rover explores. It shows only ground within {revealRadius} m of where the rover has been. Arrows at the edge of the map point toward the orbital survey leads from the landing briefing.

(2006), Science 312, 724-727; Selk crater and the Dragonfly landing site from Lorenz et al. (2021), Planet. Sci. J. 2:24, and the IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature. The dunes are generated, not real elevation.

survey._owner: T5. Lead ids match data/titan/tuning.json survey.leads. Directions and distances are computed, so the text names none. Lead texts fact-checked by research (R).
survey._sources: Interdunes: Lorenz et al. 2021, Planet. Sci. J. 2:24; Radebaugh et al. 2008, Icarus 194:690. Dunes: Radebaugh et al. 2008. Selk and its ejecta: Lorenz et al. 2021 (Cassini RADAR and radiometry); IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature, Selk.
survey.intro: Cassini radar maps show areas of interest near the landing site. Directions and distances are measured from the lander and are approximate: radar maps of Titan locate areas, not exact sites. The rover's own survey locates each site; until then, an arrow at the edge of the map points toward each area.

patch.name: Bright interdune patch
patch.source: Cassini radar suggests firm, sand-free flats between some of the dunes, probably bedrock or ice. Dragonfly's scientists picked flats like these for landing.

crest.name: Dune crest viewpoint
crest.source: Cassini radar shows the dunes as long dark stripes. From a dune crest, the rover can look out across the dune field.

ejecta.name: Selk ejecta field
ejecta.source: Cassini radar shows rough ground around Selk crater, and its microwave data point to water ice in the ejecta thrown out by the impact.

selk.name: Selk crater rim
selk.source: The crater Dragonfly will fly toward, about 80 km across. Its low rim is beyond the horizon and hidden by haze.

titanCampaign.solarNote: Solar panels give almost no power at Titan. In this version the rover runs on its battery alone.
titanCampaign.solarIncome: Solar income at Titan {income} energy/s (almost none)
facts: Titan is Saturn's largest moon. Its air is thick and mostly nitrogen: the pressure at the ground is about 1.5 times Earth's.
It is about −179 °C, day and night. Methane, a gas on Earth, can fall as rain here.
Gravity is 1.35 m/s², about one-seventh of Earth's and a little less than the Moon's.
Orange haze lets through little sunlight. Daytime at the ground is darker than Earth just after sunset.
titanCampaign.selk: The site is near Dragonfly's landing region, on its route to Selk, an impact crater about 80 km across where liquid water may once have mixed with organic material. Selk's center is about {distance} km {direction} of the lander, hidden in the haze.
dragonfly: NASA is sending a spacecraft to this region, and it will not drive. Dragonfly is a rotorcraft: a lander with eight rotors that flies from site to site.
Titan's thick air and low gravity make flying easier than driving there. A flight can cover many kilometers in under an hour and passes over the dunes instead of crossing soft sand.
Dragonfly is nuclear-powered. A radioisotope generator charges its battery during the long Titan night, and the generator's waste heat keeps the inside warm.
Launch is planned for no earlier than July 2028, with arrival at Titan in late 2034. Over its mission it will fly toward Selk crater.

titanCampaign.lesson: The right vehicle depends on the world. On the Moon and Mars, wheels work well. On Titan, thick air and low gravity favor flight.

complete.lessonsHeading: What each world asked of the rover
lessons: The Moon: mass against cost. Every kilogram and every unit of size counted toward the launch ticket.
Mars: a sunlight budget that changed every sol, with cold nights and a dust storm.
Titan: no useful sunlight, a fixed battery budget and constant cold. The real mission there flies.
